title: Graphics, GUIs, games and fun libraries

graphics_canvas.notes: Library-independent graphics skills (coordinates, bounding boxes, loops of shapes, colours, animation and wall bouncing), all checkable as plain arithmetic so they run on any platform. Library APIs live in lib_stanford_graphics, lib_turtle, lib_tkinter and lib_pygame. Colours own RGB/hex conversion (B13 deferred random colours here). Collisions between objects are collision_detection.

lib_turtle.notes: 100 Days of Code Days 18-23. turtle is in the standard library (no pip). Turtle snippets were not run on screen; positions and headings were checked with turtle.TNavigator (the turtle's movement maths without a window), which also lets a platform grade 'predict the final position' items headlessly. Collisions in turtle games (distance() < n, wall and paddle checks) are collision_detection; scoreboards and game state are game_development. Snake-body and anti-reverse KPs run as plain lists.

lib_stanford_graphics.notes: Code in Place's graphics.Canvas (a browser-side library). Snippets were not run here (library not installable); method names follow the Code in Place handout (create_rectangle/oval/line/text, move, moveto, get_left_x, get_top_y, get_canvas_width, get_last_click). Point-in-rectangle hit tests for clicks are collision_detection.rectangles_and_responses.

lib_tkinter.notes: 100 Days of Code Days 27-31. tkinter is standard library but opens a window, so snippets were not run (only the mm:ss formatting KP was). The *args/**kwargs material of Day 27 is B08 args_kwargs. Data persistence in the Password Manager / Flash Card apps (json, pandas) is B10/B18. Images on a Tk Canvas (PhotoImage) were left out; Pillow images are lib_pillow.

event_driven_programming.notes: Library-independent and fully runnable: events are simulated with dicts of handlers and a list as the event queue. The library bindings (turtle onkey/onclick, tkinter command=/bind/after, pygame.event.get) are taught in lib_turtle, lib_tkinter and lib_pygame, which depend on these topics. Web request handlers (Flask routes, B16/B17) are the same idea and could encompass callbacks_and_registration in a stitch.

game_development.notes: Project-shaped: Snake, Pong, Turtle Crossing, Breakout, Space Invaders, Asteroids and Helsinki's own game are best delivered as multisteps built on these topics plus game_loop, collision_detection and a library (lib_turtle or lib_pygame). These four topics teach the reusable pieces in plain Python so they can be graded headlessly. Text games with random (guessing games) are B13 random_module.random_games.

lib_pygame.notes: Helsinki Part 13-14 and Boot.dev Asteroids. pygame was not installed, so snippets were not run; API names follow the pygame 2 docs. The library-independent ideas (game loop, dt, vectors, collisions) live in game_loop and collision_detection, so these topics only add the pygame calls. Sound, fonts (pygame.font) and Rect methods beyond colliderect were left out.

game_loop.notes: Library-independent; loops are simulated with lists of events and dt values so they run headlessly. pygame's Clock and event queue are taught in lib_pygame, which game_loop does not require. Turtle's tracer/update version is lib_turtle.smooth_animation_and_snake.

collision_detection.notes: Pure maths, runnable without a library. Trig (sin, cos, radians), which B13 math_module left to the games batch, is vectors_and_movement KP4. Wall bouncing is graphics_canvas.animation_loop; snake self-collision is lib_turtle.smooth_animation_and_snake KP4.

lib_pillow.notes: CS50P Week 6 (P-Shirt), MIT PS5 and 100 Days image projects. Pillow was not installed, so API snippets were not run; arithmetic KPs were. Pixel arithmetic itself is image_processing (runnable on nested lists). The B10 handoff (binary images with PIL) is open_resize_save, which lists file_io.encodings_and_binary as a prerequisite.

image_processing.notes: Pixel arithmetic on nested lists, independent of Pillow so it runs and grades headlessly; lib_pillow.pixel_data connects it to real image files. NumPy image arrays (100 Days Day 77) are B18 lib_numpy.

lib_cowsay.notes: Introduced only, as CS50P's first pip-install demo; one KP (KP1) in the shared fun-output topic. Installing packages is B13 third_party_packages.

lib_emoji.notes: One KP (KP2) in the shared fun-output topic (CS50P 'Emojize').

lib_pyfiglet.notes: One shared topic for the three CS50P 'fun output' libraries (cowsay, emoji, pyfiglet), one KP each plus the argv font-choice KP; owned here because pyfiglet carries the most skill. None was installed, so output was described from the docs, not run.

lib_inflect.notes: CS50P 'Adieu, Adieu' and 'Seasons of Love'. Not installed; outputs follow the inflect docs.

lib_tabulate.notes: CS50P 'Pizza Py'. Not installed; the sample table follows tabulate's documented 'simple' format. PrettyTable (100 Days) is B13 third_party_packages.learn_from_docs.

lib_fpdf.notes: CS50P 'CS50 Shirtificate'. Uses fpdf2's current cell(text=...) spelling (older versions used txt=). Not installed; only the centring arithmetic was run.

lib_validators.notes: CS50P 'Response Validation' (validators or validator-collection). Regex validation itself is B13 regular_expressions.anchors_and_validation, which this topic depends on. validator-collection's raising style (validators.email raises on failure; checkers.is_email returns bool) was not given a KP.

topics.title: Screen coordinates: where a shape goes
topics.summary: Locate points on a canvas whose origin is the top-left corner with y growing downwards, describe a shape by its bounding box, centre a shape, and convert from centre-origin (turtle/maths) coordinates.

knowledge_points.title: The origin is the top-left corner and y grows downwards
knowledge_points.worked_example:
WIDTH, HEIGHT = 400, 300
print(WIDTH - 1, HEIGHT - 1)  # 399 299: the bottom-right pixel
print(200 > 50)  # True: (10, 200) is LOWER on screen than (10, 50)
On a canvas, x counts pixels from the left edge and y counts pixels down from the top edge.
knowledge_points.practice: Given points on a 400x300 canvas, say which is higher, lower, further left; give the coordinates of each corner and of the centre.

knowledge_points.title: A rectangle or oval is a bounding box (x1, y1, x2, y2)
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x, y, size = 50, 20, 30
box = (x, y, x + size, y + size)
print(box)  # (50, 20, 80, 50)
(x1, y1) is the top-left corner and (x2, y2) the bottom-right; an oval is drawn inside its box.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the box for a square or rectangle given its top-left corner and size; read width and height back from a box.

knowledge_points.title: Centring a shape on the canvas
knowledge_points.worked_example:
WIDTH, HEIGHT = 400, 300
size = 30
left = (WIDTH - size) // 2
top = (HEIGHT - size) // 2
print(left, top)  # 185 135
Subtract the shape's size from the canvas size and halve it; centring the top-left corner itself (200, 150) is the common bug.
knowledge_points.practice: Compute the top-left corner that centres a shape; spot the bug that puts the corner, not the shape, in the middle.

knowledge_points.title: Converting centre-origin, y-up coordinates to the screen
knowledge_points.worked_example:
WIDTH, HEIGHT = 400, 300

def to_screen(x, y):
    return x + WIDTH // 2, HEIGHT // 2 - y

print(to_screen(0, 0))     # (200, 150)
print(to_screen(100, 50))  # (300, 100)
Turtle graphics and maths put (0, 0) in the middle with y going up; screens flip y.
knowledge_points.practice: Convert points both ways; predict where a point with negative y appears.

topics.title: Rows and grids of shapes with loops and helper functions
topics.summary: Compute the positions of evenly spaced shapes with a loop or nested loop, wrap a shape in a helper function with parameters, and work out how many shapes fit.

knowledge_points.title: A row of shapes: x = i * (size + gap)
knowledge_points.worked_example:
size, gap = 40, 10
for i in range(4):
    x = i * (size + gap)
    print(x)
# 0
# 50
# 100
# 150
In a real program each x goes into canvas.create_rectangle(x, y, x + size, y + size, ...).
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the x of the n-th shape; fill in the formula for a given spacing.

knowledge_points.title: A grid: the outer loop picks the row, the inner loop the column
knowledge_points.worked_example:
size = 50
for row in range(2):
    for col in range(2):
        print(row, col, (col * size, row * size))
# 0 0 (0, 0)
# 0 1 (50, 0)
# 1 0 (0, 50)
# 1 1 (50, 50)
x comes from the column and y from the row; swapping them draws the grid sideways.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the top-left corner of a given cell; fix code that uses row for x.

knowledge_points.title: A helper function with parameters draws one shape anywhere
knowledge_points.practice: Write a helper for a centred circle's box (cx - r, cy - r, cx + r, cy + r); call it in a loop.

knowledge_points.title: How many shapes fit, and the last one off the edge
knowledge_points.worked_example:
WIDTH, size, gap = 400, 40, 10
n = (WIDTH + gap) // (size + gap)
print(n)  # 8
last_x2 = (n - 1) * (size + gap) + size
print(last_x2 <= WIDTH)  # True
The last shape needs no gap after it, hence WIDTH + gap; check x2 <= WIDTH before drawing.
knowledge_points.practice: Compute how many shapes fit for given sizes; predict whether the last one is cut off.

topics.title: Colours: names, RGB tuples, hex codes and random colours
topics.summary: Describe colours as names, RGB tuples and #RRGGBB strings, convert between RGB and hex, and pick random colours safely.

knowledge_points.title: Colour names and a random pick
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import random
COLORS = ['red', 'orange', 'green', 'blue']
color = random.choice(COLORS)
print(color in COLORS)  # True
Graphics libraries accept common colour names as strings; random.choice picks one per shape.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which values a random colour expression can produce.

knowledge_points.title: RGB tuples: three numbers from 0 to 255
knowledge_points.worked_example:
RED = (255, 0, 0)
YELLOW = (255, 255, 0)  # red + green light
print(YELLOW[1])  # 255
print(max((0, 0, 0)), min((255, 255, 255)))  # 0 255: black, white
Each number is the amount of red, green and blue light; (0, 0, 0) is black, (255, 255, 255) white.
knowledge_points.practice: Match tuples to colour names (black, white, grey, yellow); write the tuple for a described colour.

knowledge_points.title: Hex codes #RRGGBB
knowledge_points.worked_example:
r, g, b = 255, 165, 0
print(f'#{r:02x}{g:02x}{b:02x}')  # #ffa500
print(int('a5', 16))  # 165
:02x writes a number as two hex digits; int(text, 16) reads them back.
knowledge_points.practice: Convert RGB to hex and hex to RGB; find the bug when :x without 02 gives a 5-character code.

knowledge_points.title: Random RGB colours and keeping values in range
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import random
random.seed(1)
color = (random.randint(0, 255), random.randint(0, 255), random.randint(0, 255))
print(color)  # (68, 32, 130)
brighter = min(255, color[0] + 200)
print(brighter)  # 255
randint includes 255; when you adjust a channel, clamp it with min/max so it stays 0-255.
knowledge_points.practice: Write a random-colour helper; clamp adjusted channels; predict a seeded colour.

topics.title: Animation: move a little, pause, repeat
topics.summary: Animate a shape by changing its position by a velocity each frame, stop at an edge, and bounce off walls by reversing the velocity.

knowledge_points.title: A frame is a small move followed by a short pause
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import time
x = 0
for frame in range(3):
    x += 10
    print(x)  # the real program redraws here
    time.sleep(0.05)
# 10
# 20
# 30
Many tiny moves with pauses look like motion; without the pause it finishes before you see it.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the position after n frames; choose what happens when the sleep is removed.

knowledge_points.title: Velocity on both axes: dx and dy
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x, y, dx, dy = 0, 100, 5, -2
for frame in range(4):
    x += dx
    y += dy
print(x, y)  # 20 92
dy < 0 moves up the screen because y grows downwards.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace x and y over frames in a trace table; choose dx, dy for a given direction.

knowledge_points.title: Stop when the shape reaches the edge
knowledge_points.worked_example:
WIDTH, size = 100, 20
x = 0
while x + size < WIDTH:
    x += 15
print(x)  # 90: past the edge!
Test the right edge x + size, and check before moving (or clamp) so the shape never ends past WIDTH.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict where the loop stops; fix the condition or clamp so the shape ends exactly at the edge.

knowledge_points.title: Bounce: reverse the velocity at a wall
knowledge_points.worked_example:
WIDTH, size = 100, 20
x, dx = 60, 10
for frame in range(5):
    x += dx
    if x <= 0 or x + size >= WIDTH:
        dx = -dx
    print(x, dx)
# 70 10
# 80 -10
# 70 -10
# 60 -10
# 50 -10
Flipping the sign of dx sends the shape back; the top and bottom walls flip dy the same way.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace a bouncing shape; write the condition for the floor and ceiling.

topics.title: Drawing on the Code in Place Canvas
topics.summary: Create a Canvas and draw rectangles, ovals, lines and text with create_* calls that take corner coordinates.

knowledge_points.title: Make a canvas and draw a rectangle from two corners
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from graphics import Canvas
canvas = Canvas(400, 300)
canvas.create_rectangle(50, 20, 80, 50, 'blue')
The four numbers are x1, y1, x2, y2, not x, y, width, height: this square is 30 pixels wide.
knowledge_points.practice: Give the call that draws a described rectangle; fix a call that passes width and height as x2, y2.

knowledge_points.title: Ovals and circles fill their bounding box
knowledge_points.worked_example:
cx, cy, r = 200, 150, 25
canvas.create_oval(cx - r, cy - r, cx + r, cy + r, 'red')
To draw a circle around a centre, step r left/up for the first corner and r right/down for the second.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the create_oval call for a circle with a given centre and radius; predict the circle's centre from a call.

knowledge_points.title: Lines, text and colours inside loops
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import random
for i in range(5):
    color = random.choice(['red', 'green', 'blue'])
    canvas.create_line(0, i * 20, 400, i * 20, color)
canvas.create_text(10, 10, text='Score: 0')
A line is two endpoints; text needs a position and a text= keyword. Loops and random colours work as in plain Python.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the endpoints of each line a loop draws; write a loop that draws a flag's stripes.

topics.title: Moving shapes and reading clicks on the Canvas
topics.summary: Keep the id a create_* call returns, move the shape with move/moveto, read its position back, and react to mouse clicks in an animation loop.

knowledge_points.title: create_* returns an id; move is relative, moveto is absolute
knowledge_points.worked_example:
ball = canvas.create_oval(0, 0, 20, 20, 'red')
canvas.move(ball, 10, 5)     # now at (10, 5)
canvas.move(ball, 10, 5)     # now at (20, 10)
canvas.moveto(ball, 100, 0)  # now at (100, 0)
Keep the id in a variable: it is the only way to change that shape later.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the top-left corner after a sequence of move/moveto calls.

knowledge_points.title: Reading the position back to bounce
knowledge_points.worked_example:
dx = 10
while True:
    canvas.move(ball, dx, 0)
    if canvas.get_left_x(ball) + 20 >= canvas.get_canvas_width():
        dx = -dx
    time.sleep(0.05)
get_left_x / get_top_y report where the shape is now, so the bounce test needs no separate x variable.
knowledge_points.practice: Complete the bounce condition for the left wall and the floor; trace positions for a few frames.

knowledge_points.title: Clicks: get_last_click returns (x, y) or None
knowledge_points.worked_example:
while True:
    click = canvas.get_last_click()
    if click is not None:
        x, y = click
        canvas.create_oval(x - 5, y - 5, x + 5, y + 5, 'black')
    time.sleep(0.05)
No click since the last check gives None; unpacking None would raise TypeError, so test first.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix a loop that unpacks the click without checking for None; predict the dot's box for a click at (40, 60).

topics.title: Callbacks: register a function now, run it later
topics.summary: Register handler functions for named events in a dictionary, fire events to call them, and avoid passing a function's result instead of the function.

knowledge_points.title: Registering does not run the handler
knowledge_points.worked_example:
handlers = {}

def on(event, handler):
    handlers[event] = handler

def jump():
    print('jump!')

on('space', jump)
print('registered')
handlers['space']()
# registered
# jump!
on() only stores the function; it runs when the event is fired. GUI libraries' onkey, command= and bind work this way.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the order of printed lines when handlers are registered and later fired.

knowledge_points.title: Pass the function, not its result
knowledge_points.worked_example:
on('space', jump())
# jump!   <- printed immediately, while registering
handlers['space']()
# TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
jump() runs straight away and returns None, so None is what gets stored.
knowledge_points.practice: Find the bug in a registration line; predict what is printed and when.

knowledge_points.title: Firing an event safely: ignore events nobody handles
knowledge_points.practice: Write fire(); predict output for a sequence of handled and unhandled events.

knowledge_points.title: Several handlers for one event
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output order; add a handler so a given output appears.

topics.title: The event loop: waiting for events and dispatching them
topics.summary: Explain how an event-driven program differs from a top-to-bottom one, trace an event loop that dispatches a queue of events to handlers that share state, and see why a slow handler freezes everything.

knowledge_points.title: The program waits; events decide what runs next
knowledge_points.worked_example:
events = ['right', 'right', 'left']
x = 0
for event in events:   # stands in for the library's loop
    if event == 'right':
        x += 10
    elif event == 'left':
        x -= 10
print(x)  # 10
A console program asks questions in its own order; a GUI or game runs a loop that waits for the user's next event (mainloop(), the game loop).
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the final state for an event sequence; choose which programs are event-driven.

knowledge_points.title: Dispatching through a handler table until a quit event
knowledge_points.practice: Trace which handlers run for an event queue; fill in the dispatch line.

knowledge_points.title: Handlers share state between events
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the shared state after events; fix a handler that forgets global and raises UnboundLocalError.

knowledge_points.title: A slow handler freezes the whole program
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def on_click():
    time.sleep(5)   # nothing else can run for 5 seconds
    print('done')
Only one handler runs at a time; while it sleeps or loops, the event loop cannot redraw or react. Use the library's timer (after(), ontimer) instead.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which handler makes the window stop responding; reorder code to use a timer instead of a sleeping loop.

topics.title: Event data: handlers that receive arguments
topics.summary: Write handlers whose parameters match what the library passes (coordinates or an event object), pass extra data with lambda without the late-binding trap, and use bound methods as handlers.

knowledge_points.title: The library decides the arguments
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def on_click(x, y):
    print('clicked at', x, y)

click_handler = on_click
click_handler(30, 40)  # clicked at 30 40

def bad_click():
    print('hi')
click_handler = bad_click
click_handler(30, 40)
# TypeError: bad_click() takes 0 positional arguments but 2 were given
Turtle's onclick passes (x, y); tkinter's bind passes one event object; turtle's onkey passes nothing. Match the signature.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose the right signature for a given registration; read the TypeError and fix the handler.

knowledge_points.title: Event objects carry details as attributes
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what a handler prints for given event objects.

knowledge_points.title: Passing extra data with lambda, and the loop trap
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def choose(n):
    print('chose', n)

buttons = []
for n in range(3):
    buttons.append(lambda: choose(n))
buttons[0]()  # chose 2  (!)

buttons = []
for n in range(3):
    buttons.append(lambda n=n: choose(n))
buttons[0]()  # chose 0
A handler takes no arguments, so lambda wraps the call; n=n freezes the current value for each button.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which value each handler uses; fix a loop of button callbacks.

knowledge_points.title: A bound method is a ready-made handler
knowledge_points.practice: Predict object state after events; register the right paddle's method for the arrow keys.

topics.title: Turtle graphics: moving and turning
topics.summary: Create a Turtle, move it with forward/backward/goto, turn it with left/right/setheading, and predict its final position and heading on a centre-origin, y-up plane.

knowledge_points.title: A turtle starts at (0, 0) facing east
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from turtle import Turtle, Screen
tim = Turtle()
tim.forward(100)
print(tim.position())  # (100.00,0.00)
(0, 0) is the centre of the window and the turtle draws a line as it moves.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the position after one or two forward/backward calls.

knowledge_points.title: left turns anticlockwise, right clockwise; y goes up
knowledge_points.worked_example:
tim.forward(100)
tim.left(90)
tim.forward(50)
print(tim.position(), tim.heading())  # (100.00,50.00) 90.0
Heading 0 is east, 90 north, 180 west, 270 south. Unlike a canvas, positive y is UP.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace position and heading through a sequence of moves; predict the final position.

knowledge_points.title: Jumping with goto and setheading
knowledge_points.worked_example:
tim.goto(50, -20)
tim.setheading(180)
tim.forward(10)
print(tim.xcor(), tim.ycor())  # 40.0 -20.0
goto ignores the heading; setheading sets an absolute direction, unlike left/right which turn relative to the current one.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict coordinates after mixed goto/setheading/forward calls; choose setheading vs left for a task.

knowledge_points.title: Diagonal moves give float positions
knowledge_points.worked_example:
tim.left(45)
tim.forward(100)
print(round(tim.xcor(), 2), round(tim.ycor(), 2))  # 70.71 70.71
Positions are floats; round before comparing, e.g. tim.xcor() > 230 rather than == 230.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict rounded coordinates after a 45-degree move; fix a check that uses == on a float position.

topics.title: Turtle drawings: polygons, pen up/down and colours
topics.summary: Draw regular polygons and patterns with loops, lift the pen to move without drawing, set colours (including RGB with colormode(255)) and lay out a grid of dots.

knowledge_points.title: Polygons: n sides, turn 360 / n
knowledge_points.worked_example:
for _ in range(3):
    tim.forward(50)
    tim.left(120)
print(round(tim.xcor()), round(tim.ycor()), tim.heading())  # 0 0 0.0
The turns of any closed shape add up to 360, so a triangle turns 120 and the turtle ends where it began.
knowledge_points.practice: Give the turn angle for an n-sided shape; predict the final heading; write a loop drawing shapes with 3 to 10 sides.

knowledge_points.title: penup and pendown: moving without drawing
knowledge_points.worked_example:
for _ in range(10):
    tim.pendown()
    tim.forward(10)
    tim.penup()
    tim.forward(10)
# a dashed line of 10 dashes; the turtle ends at (200, 0)
With the pen up the turtle still moves; only the line is skipped.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the number of dashes and the final position; reorder lines to draw a dotted line.

knowledge_points.title: Colours: names, and RGB tuples after colormode(255)
knowledge_points.worked_example:
screen = Screen()
screen.colormode(255)
tim.color((255, 165, 0))
tim.pensize(5)
tim.speed('fastest')
Without colormode(255) turtle expects RGB values from 0 to 1 and raises an error for (255, 165, 0).
knowledge_points.practice: Fix a program that passes 0-255 tuples without colormode; write a random walk that picks a random colour and heading (0, 90, 180 or 270) each step.

knowledge_points.title: A grid of dots (the Hirst painting)
knowledge_points.worked_example:
tim.penup()
for row in range(3):
    tim.goto(-100, -100 + row * 50)
    for col in range(5):
        tim.dot(20, 'red')
        tim.forward(50)
goto starts each row at the left; dot() draws without the pen. After the loops the turtle is at (150, 0).
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the final position; change the loops to make a 10 x 10 grid.

topics.title: Turtle events: keys, clicks and pop-up prompts
topics.summary: Make a turtle program respond to keys with listen()/onkey, to clicks with onclick handlers that take (x, y), and ask the user for input with textinput.

knowledge_points.title: listen, onkey, and keeping the window open
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def move_forward():
    tim.forward(10)

screen.listen()
screen.onkey(move_forward, 'w')
screen.exitonclick()
listen() gives the window keyboard focus; exitonclick() (or mainloop()) keeps the program running so events can arrive.
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the lines of an Etch-A-Sketch program; fix onkey(move_forward(), 'w').

knowledge_points.title: Key handlers that turn and clear
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def turn_left():
    tim.setheading(tim.heading() + 10)

def clear():
    tim.clear()
    tim.penup()
    tim.home()
    tim.pendown()

screen.onkey(turn_left, 'a')
screen.onkey(clear, 'c')
Each key gets its own small function; key names include 'Up', 'Left', 'space'.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the heading after pressing keys in a given order.

knowledge_points.title: Click handlers receive the coordinates
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def jump_to(x, y):
    tim.goto(x, y)

screen.onclick(jump_to)
onclick calls jump_to(x, y) with the click position in turtle coordinates; a handler with no parameters raises TypeError on the first click.
knowledge_points.practice: Write a click handler that stamps a dot where the user clicks; read the error from a wrong signature.

knowledge_points.title: Asking the user: textinput returns a string or None
knowledge_points.worked_example:
bet = screen.textinput('Make your bet', 'Which turtle will win? Enter a colour:')
if bet is not None:
    bet = bet.lower()
Cancel gives None, so check before calling string methods; numinput returns a float.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the value of bet for typed input and for Cancel; fix code that crashes on Cancel.

topics.title: Many turtles: lists of turtles and Turtle subclasses
topics.summary: Keep several Turtle objects in a list, each with its own state, and build game pieces (ball, paddle, car) as subclasses of Turtle with their own attributes and methods.

knowledge_points.title: A list of turtles: each keeps its own position
knowledge_points.worked_example:

knowledge_points.title: Images: load once, blit every frame

robot = pygame.image.load('robot.png')
x = 640 - robot.get_width()

topics.title: Images as grids of RGB pixels
topics.summary: Treat an image as a grid of (r, g, b) tuples and compute new images: greyscale, negative and brightness changes clamped to 0-255.

knowledge_points.title: A pixel is an (r, g, b) tuple at image[y][x]
knowledge_points.worked_example:
image = [[(255, 0, 0), (0, 0, 0)],
         [(0, 255, 0), (255, 255, 255)]]
height, width = len(image), len(image[0])
print(width, height, image[1][0])  # 2 2 (0, 255, 0)
Rows are y (top to bottom), positions in a row are x.

knowledge_points.title: Greyscale: average the three channels
knowledge_points.practice: Compute grey values for pixels; write the weighted version with round().

knowledge_points.title: A filter builds a new grid pixel by pixel
knowledge_points.worked_example:
image = [[(255, 0, 0), (0, 0, 0)], [(0, 255, 0), (255, 255, 255)]]
negative = []
for row in image:
    new_row = []
    for r, g, b in row:
        new_row.append((255 - r, 255 - g, 255 - b))
    negative.append(new_row)
print(negative[0])  # [(0, 255, 255), (255, 255, 255)]
Tuples cannot be changed, so build new pixels; the loop shape is the same for every per-pixel filter.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the result of a filter on a small grid; reorder the lines of a filter.

knowledge_points.title: Clamping: keep channels between 0 and 255

topics.title: Colour-matrix filters, flips and blurs
topics.summary: Apply a 3x3 colour matrix to every pixel (as in colour-blindness simulation), flip and rotate images with slicing and transposing, and blur by averaging neighbours with edge handling.

knowledge_points.title: A colour matrix mixes the channels
knowledge_points.worked_example:
M = [[0.567, 0.433, 0],
     [0.558, 0.442, 0],
     [0, 0.242, 0.758]]
r, g, b = 200, 100, 50
new = []
for i in range(3):
    new.append(round(M[i][0] * r + M[i][1] * g + M[i][2] * b))
print(new)  # [157, 156, 62]
Each new channel is a weighted sum of the old r, g, b (MIT's colour-blindness filters).
knowledge_points.practice: Compute one filtered pixel by hand; write the per-pixel function.

knowledge_points.title: Flips with slicing
knowledge_points.worked_example:
image = [[1, 2, 3],
         [4, 5, 6]]
mirror = [row[::-1] for row in image]
upside_down = image[::-1]
print(mirror)       # [[3, 2, 1], [6, 5, 4]]
print(upside_down)  # [[4, 5, 6], [1, 2, 3]]
Numbers stand in for pixels; reversing each row mirrors left-right, reversing the list of rows flips top-bottom.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict flipped grids; choose the expression for a given flip.

knowledge_points.title: Rotating a quarter turn: transpose, then mirror
knowledge_points.worked_example:
image = [[1, 2, 3],
         [4, 5, 6]]
turned = []
for c in range(len(image[0])):
    col = [row[c] for row in image]
    turned.append(col[::-1])
print(turned)  # [[4, 1], [5, 2], [6, 3]]
Each column, read bottom to top, becomes a row: a clockwise quarter turn, and width and height swap.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the rotated grid; fix a version that rotates the wrong way.

knowledge_points.title: Blur: average a pixel with its neighbours
knowledge_points.worked_example:
grid = [[0, 0, 0],
        [0, 90, 0],
        [0, 0, 0]]
def blur_at(g, y, x):
    vals = [g[j][i] for j in range(y - 1, y + 2) for i in range(x - 1, x + 2)
            if 0 <= j < len(g) and 0 <= i < len(g[0])]
    return sum(vals) // len(vals)
print(blur_at(grid, 1, 1), blur_at(grid, 0, 0))  # 10 22
Edge pixels have fewer neighbours, so divide by how many were actually inside the image.
knowledge_points.practice: Compute blurred values at centre, edge and corner; fix a blur that crashes or wraps at the edges.

topics.title: Hiding messages in the lowest bits of pixels
topics.summary: Read and set the least significant bit of a channel, reveal a hidden black-and-white image, and hide and recover text one bit per pixel (steganography).

knowledge_points.title: The lowest bit barely changes a colour
knowledge_points.worked_example:
v = 182
print(v % 2)            # 0: the lowest bit
print(v - v % 2 + 1)    # 183: lowest bit set to 1
Changing the last bit changes the value by at most 1, which no eye can see.
knowledge_points.practice: Read the lowest bit of several values; set it to 0 or 1.

knowledge_points.title: Revealing a hidden black-and-white image
knowledge_points.worked_example:
row = [182, 37, 200, 91]
revealed = [255 if v % 2 else 0 for v in row]
print(revealed)  # [0, 255, 0, 255]
Scale each lowest bit up to full black or white and the hidden picture appears (MIT problem set 5).
knowledge_points.practice: Reveal small grids; fix a version that keeps the original values.

knowledge_points.title: Hiding text: one bit per pixel
knowledge_points.worked_example:
bits = format(ord('H'), '08b')
print(bits)  # 01001000
pixels = [100, 101, 102, 103, 104, 105, 106, 107]
hidden = []
for i in range(8):
    hidden.append(pixels[i] - pixels[i] % 2 + int(bits[i]))
print(hidden)  # [100, 101, 102, 102, 105, 104, 106, 106]
Each pixel's lowest bit now holds one bit of the letter; no value moved by more than 1.
knowledge_points.practice: Hide a letter in given pixels; predict the changed values.

knowledge_points.title: Recovering the text
knowledge_points.worked_example:
hidden = [100, 101, 102, 102, 105, 104, 106, 106]
bits = ''
for p in hidden:
    bits += str(p % 2)
print(bits, chr(int(bits, 2)))  # 01001000 H
Read 8 lowest bits, turn them into a number with int(bits, 2), then a character with chr.
knowledge_points.practice: Decode letters from pixel lists; fix a decoder that reads the bits in the wrong order.

small = img.resize((320, 240))
turned = img.rotate(90)
face = img.crop((100, 50, 300, 250))   # (left, top, right, bottom)
